Issued at 516 AM CDT Tue Aug 4 2026

What is left of the mid-level ridge axis has passed into the Great 
Lakes Region, which has left a WAA regime and higher theta-e 
transport into the lower Missouri River Valley. Short-wave trough 
and notable vort maxima over the Northern Plains and Canadian 
Prairie Provinces continues to move eastward, and has dug southward. 
This has resulted in upper-level divergence across the eastern 
Plains of the Dakotas toward the Upper Midwest. This pattern has 
also created a few mid-level perturbations over the Rockies, and has 
generated enough dCVA to provide lift to develop a surface cyclone. 
As this has deepened, surface pressure falls have already been 
extending eastward into portions of eastern Kansas this morning. 
Over the Northern Rockies this a strong surface anticyclone is 
developing behind the northern short-wave that has been breaking 
down the ridge pattern. This is pushing a cold front across the 
Plains, and overnight produced rain showers across parts of Nebraska 
and Kansas. So far those have been on a downward trend, but may be 
enough to result in sprinkle activity in far northwestern Missouri 
this morning and afternoon. We will likely see increasing cloud 
cover from the Plains activity later today, though we may get a 
period of subsidence that helps to create breaks in the cloud cover. 
With the deepening cyclone, low-level flow remains southerly, and 
will provide WAA boosting temperatures into the 90s across most of 
the forecast area. Far northwestern Missouri may stay in the upper 
80s, as cloud cover may be more dense there. While there will 
increasing surface convergence, mid-level kinematic support will be 
lacking across forecast area for most of the afternoon, and 
therefore will maintain a mostly dry forecast. However a healthy 
instability axis is progged to setup across the area, that will set 
the stage precipitation late Tuesday Night, and spreading across 
most of the area Wednesday. 

H5 height falls will pick up in pace late Tuesday evening, and the 
surface cyclone will begin to track toward Central Kansas, with 
inverted surface trough extending northeastward into north-central 
Missouri. The cold front will continue to trail the cyclone. Recent 
CAM runs have delayed the timing of rain shower activity late 
tonight, not entering northern Missouri until after 04z. Most of 
this activity is expected to be elevated, with a strong inversion in 
place. Mid-level cooling though may help to steepen 700-500mb lapse 
rates, and with increasing shear could try to help some activity 
organize. But overall, the environment late tonight may struggle to 
support stronger storms. Wednesday morning, we may start to see 
activity spread as the cyclone continues to deepen and surface 
convergence increases in strength. However, as the forcing moves 
eastward, the instability may be very meager. Currently the HRRR is 
only depicting a few hundred J/kg of CAPE throughout the warm 
sector, which may keep updrafts fairly week. However, deep warm 
cloud processes and PWATs in the warm sector of 1.65 inches could 
allow even general shower activity to very efficient with rainfall 
production, which may result in hydro issues even Wednesday morning. 
Attention then turns to the afternoon, to see if any clearing can 
occur after elevated morning activity. It is possible with the H5 
pattern we may have be able to induce subsidence late in the morning 
and early afternoon, that will allow the boundary layer to 
destabilize, while surface cyclone continues to deepen and more 
moisture transport occurs into the lower Missouri River Valley. 
Surface pressure falls push east-southeast as the cold front 
continues track across the area. This will be the main forcing 
needed for activity. If the instability can be realized, bulk shear 
values near the cold front should be around 30-40 kts, aiding in 
helping convection become organized. However, with continued 
moisture transport and no EML, mid-level lapse rates may only reach 
between 5-6C/km, limiting the strength of updrafts despite having 
stronger wind shear. Precipitation loading though could be enough to 
produce wind gusts around 60 MPH with storms, especially if they 
occur during a rapid decaying phase of the storm. Overall CAPE 
profiles from model soundings late afternoon and into the evening on 
Wednesday are fairly skinny. However PWAT values ahead of the cold 
front are currently progged at over 1.80 inches with warm cloud 
depths up to nearly 4km, and may result in hydro and flooding 
issues, especially if multiple storms develop and train along the 
front. Amongst HREF members, heaviest QPF values are favored for 
northern and northeast Missouri. 00z HREF PMM values for QPF are 
nearly 2.5 to 3.0 inches in our northeastern zones, then drop off 
southward through central Missouri to the Interstate 70 corridor.
